text:
Not everyone agrees. The best evidence is mixed: Bloom et al. (*Nature*, 2024), a randomized trial of hybrid work at Trip.com, found no productivity loss and about a third lower attrition, and an earlier call-center trial found gains. A memo claiming consensus will be easy to rebut. These narrower claims are defensible:

- **Fully remote work lowered output in some settings.** Atkin, Schoar and Shinde (2023) found data-entry workers in India about 18% less productive when fully remote. Gibbs, Mengel and Siemroth (2023) found that at an Asian IT firm, hours rose while output per hour fell.
- **Remote work weakens collaboration across teams.** Yang et al. (*Nature Human Behaviour*, 2022), using Microsoft data, found firm-wide remote work made networks more siloed and reduced bridging ties between groups.
- **Remote work reduces mentoring of junior staff.** Emanuel, Harrington and Pallais (2023) found less feedback for junior engineers when working remotely, which risks slower skill development.

These are from memory, so verify the figures and citations before they go in the memo. The first two points apply to specific roles and fully remote setups, not to hybrid work generally, so frame the memo as "remote work carries specific costs" rather than "remote work kills productivity." The strongest counterargument is the Trip.com result, so the memo should address it directly.
